So would this be the same thing as an SSL certificate?

Well… yes. The whole identification part (that you’re communicating securely with whoever you wanted and not an in-the-middle attacker) of TLS is based on certificates and trust that stems from certificates granting other certificates trust through signatures.

The thing is, if you want to have a certificate that’s automatically trusted by browsers and devices in the wild, you normally need to have your own certificate signed by one of the established “trusted” (as far as machines go, at least, considering the security breaches at CAs like DigiNotar) certificate authorities whose certificates are shipped with those clients. Depending on the amount of validation of ownership of your domain and how extensive your certificate request is (for example, maybe you want a “wildcard” certificate *.example.com that’s valid for all subdomains of example.com, not just example.com itself), those CAs charge a little to very large fee to sign your certificate every 1 or 2 years. That can be a serious consideration if you want to roll out TLS (whether it be for HTTPS or secure mail, FTP etc.)

Let’s Encrypt is a new public benefit corporation that wants to roll out encrypted communication as wide as possible over the Internet, so they created their own certificate authority that will issue certificates for free in the near future. The problem is that it will take a while until Let’s Encrypt’s root certificate will be considered trusted and shipped with browsers (one of their supporters is Mozilla, so I would expect Firefox and derived browsers to be the first to include it).

They solved that by having their root certificate sign two sub-certificates X1 and X2, which in turn will be responsible for issueing end-user certificates. The already trusted IdenTrust certificate authority now cross-signed those sub-certificates as well, which means any current TLS implementation will see your Let’s Encypt-issued certificate as valid (the path of trust goes IdenTrust → Let’s Encrypt X1/X2 → your certificate). Once the Let’s Encrypt root certificate is generally considered “trusted”, your certificate’s validation will completely stem from Let’s Encrypt themselves (Let’s Encrypt Root CA → Let’s Encrypt X1/X2 → your certificate).
